title: Form labels, instructions, and error identification
learningObjectives: Explain form labels, instructions, and error identification and apply inclusive semantic HTML practices.

understand.concept: Accessible forms provide persistent labels, clear instructions, appropriate grouping, and errors associated with the relevant controls. label elements connect visible text to controls; fieldset and legend group related fields; aria-describedby can associate instructions and error messages.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear form structure reduces errors and helps users understand what information is required. Placeholders are not persistent labels, and colour alone does not identify invalid fields.
understand.analogy: A form is a conversation: each field needs a clear question, any necessary explanation, and a useful correction when the answer is not accepted.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; accessibility APIs, semantics, and assistive technology behaviour require standards-based implementation and testing.

explain.narrative: The fieldset and legend group related controls; labels name each field; the email instructions and error are associated with the input.

examples.code: <form><fieldset><legend>Contact details</legend><label for='name'>Name</label><input id='name' name='name' required><label for='email'>Email</label><input id='email' name='email' type='email' required aria-describedby='email-help email-error'><small id='email-help'>Use an address you can access.</small><small id='email-error'>Enter a valid email address.</small></fieldset></form>
examples.explanation: The fieldset and legend group related controls; labels name each field; the email instructions and error are associated with the input.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered semantic HTML example demonstrating the accessibility principle.

practise.guidedTask: Create a registration form with fieldsets, labels, instructions, required state, and field-level error messages. Test it without relying on colour.
practise.independentTask: Audit a small page using keyboard navigation and an accessibility tree. Fix semantics, labels, alternatives, and relationships without adding unnecessary ARIA.
hints: Use native HTML where it provides the required semantics.
Keep visible labels and focus indicators.
Test meaningful content with keyboard and assistive technology where available.

practice.starterCode:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Form labels, instructions, and error identification</title></head><body>
<form><fieldset><legend>Contact details</legend><label for='name'>Name</label><input id='name' name='name' required><label for='email'>Email</label><input id='email' name='email' type='email' required aria-describedby='email-help email-error'><small id='email-help'>Use an address you can access.</small><small id='email-error'>Enter a valid email address.</small></fieldset></form>
</body></html>

questions.prompt: Which element groups related form controls and provides a group caption?
questions.explanation: fieldset groups controls and legend provides the group's caption.

questions.prompt: What is a good accessibility workflow?
options: Use semantic HTML first, then add only necessary ARIA and test
Add ARIA roles to every element
questions.answer: Use semantic HTML first, then add only necessary ARIA and test
questions.explanation: Native semantics provide a strong baseline and testing reveals real interaction barriers.
